The Blackspot climbing perch Ctenopharynx intermedius attains a maximum body length of 21.0 centimeters [Li = 21.0 centimeters] in Lake Malawi, a figure documented through extensive gill-net surveys. Total length at puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal recrudescence in males, occurs at 15.5 centimeters [Lp = 15.5 centimeters], a threshold corroborated by histological examination of testicular tissue sampled across multiple breeding seasons. Female maturation appears to lag slightly behind males, though the size differential remains modest. These length-based benchmarks align closely with values reported for other members of the haplochromine flock, suggesting a conserved relationship between somatic growth and reproductive development within this cichlid lineage. The ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults reaches approximately 92 grams [Wwi = approximately 92 grams], with gravid females occasionally exceeding this figure during peak spawning months. Such mass represents a substantial investment in both somatic tissue and ovarian output, reflecting the energetic demands of iteroparous reproduction in a relatively stable lacustrine environment.

Neonatal mass in this species has been inferred from egg dimensions of related taxa, yielding an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.023 grams [Wwb = 0.023 grams]. This calculation derives from the prolate spheroid volume formula applied to typical egg lengths of 4.3 millimeters and widths of 3.2 millimeters observed in the congener Copadichromis chrysonotus. Yolk-sac larvae emerge from the demersal eggs after approximately five days of incubation at ambient lake temperatures, immediately commencing a lecithotrophic phase during which they absorb endogenous reserves. The transition to exogenous feeding begins roughly two days following larval eclosion, coinciding with the opening of the mouth and the differentiation of retinal tissues. At this stage, the prolarvae are approximately 5.5 millimeters in total length and possess a visible, though rapidly diminishing, yolk sac. Mortality during this early period is substantial, driven by predation from both invertebrate zooplankton and larger cichlids, although the precise survival fraction remains unquantified for wild populations.

Wet weight at puberty has been computed from the length-weight relationship established for Lake Malawi cichlids, with individuals reaching 37.8 grams [Wwp = 37.8 grams] at the onset of reproductive capacity. This relationship follows the standard allometric equation W = 0.01230 * L^2.93, a formula derived from extensive morphometric data collected across multiple seasons. Field records indicate that females achieve this weight approximately eight months after hatching, at which point vitellogenesis commences and the ovaries begin sequential oocyte recruitment. Histological sections of ovarian tissue from pubertal females reveal the presence of cortical alveoli and early vitellogenic oocytes, confirming physiological readiness for spawning. The onset of puberty at this body mass represents a critical life-history transition, as it marks the point at which energy allocation shifts from exclusively somatic growth toward combined growth and reproductive investment. Males tend to reach this threshold at a slightly smaller body length.

The maximum lifespan of Ctenopharynx intermedius has been estimated at 6 years [am = 6 years] when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Scale annuli counts from wild-caught specimens generally corroborate this duration, with the oldest individuals rarely exceeding five annual growth rings—a difference that likely reflects elevated mortality from predation, parasite loads, and stochastic environmental perturbations in natural settings. Senescence in this species manifests as a gradual decline in reproductive output during the final year of life, characterized by reduced clutch sizes and diminished egg viability. Comparative data from other Malawian haplochromines suggest that lifespan in the wild may be constrained by the intensity of predation pressure from piscivorous fishes such as Rhamphochromis species, as well as by the energetic costs associated with multiple spawning events within a single season.

Spawning behavior in Ctenopharynx intermedius occurs on a predictable seasonal schedule, with gravid females depositing between 15 and 25 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 15 and 25 eggs per clutch] on submerged rock surfaces within the males' defended territories. Each female typically produces three distinct spawnings over the course of the breeding season [F_R_i = three distinct spawnings over the course of the breeding season], resulting in an annual reproductive output that reflects the species' iteroparous strategy. The eggs are adhesive and measure approximately 4.3 millimeters in diameter, receiving paternal protection through fanning and guarding until larval eclosion. Brood care is exclusively maternal in this mouthbrooding species following fertilization, with females carrying developing larvae in their buccal cavity for approximately three weeks before releasing free-swimming juveniles. Environmental factors such as dissolved oxygen concentration and food availability for fry likely impose constraints on the upper limit of clutch size, as larger broods may reduce maternal foraging efficiency during the mouthbrooding period. Data from laboratory colonies indicate that female body size correlates positively with clutch volume.
